The Mathematics of Kolam

Kolam symmetry groups can be analysed at several levels: the finite point-group symmetries of individual designs, the two-colour (or multi-colour) symmetries of the associated Lunda designs, and, for repeating patterns, the wallpaper groups. The most precise recent classification for square-tile sikku kolams is due to Venkatraman Gopalan.

Point groups of square-tile sikku kolams

Gopalan (2023/2024) classifies all kolams assembled from six basic square tiles (circle, drop, eye, door, fan, diamond) into exactly eight point groups. These are the crystallographic-style point groups compatible with the square grid and the three traditional rules (every pulli encircled, discrete crossings, no loose ends):

Point group Symmetries Notes
\(4mm_d\) 4-fold rotation + edge-parallel mirrors + diagonal mirrors Highest possible; any two of the three operations generate the third
\(4\) 4-fold rotation only
\(2mm\) 2-fold rotation + two orthogonal edge-parallel mirrors
\(2m_{d}m_{d}\) 2-fold rotation + two orthogonal diagonal mirrors
\(2\) 2-fold rotation only
\(m\) Single edge-parallel mirror
\(m_d\) Single diagonal mirror Distinguished from for artistic reasons
\(1\) Identity only No non-trivial symmetry

Symmetry groups per Gopalan

All operations fix the centre. The classification is exhaustive for these tiles; higher or “exotic” symmetries do not appear. Enumeration formulae are given for two standard templates (single rectangle and two interlocked rectangles) by counting the free shared edges that must be specified once the symmetry is imposed.

Download PDF File

Mirror curves and Lunda designs

Paulus Gerdes’ treatment of Tchokwe sona and related Tamil kolams emphasises mirror curves: 45° rays reflecting off internal and boundary mirrors. Many traditional monolinear examples possess 2-fold or 4-fold rotational symmetry, and some also possess reflection axes. The associated Lunda designs (black/white or multi-colour colourings of the unit squares traversed by the curve) obey strong local and global two-colour symmetries:

  • equal numbers of black and white squares in every row and every column,
  • border and nearest-neighbour parity constraints.

These are not full wallpaper groups; they are finite (or rectangular) designs with prescribed two-colour balance. Gerdes proved that any rectangular colouring satisfying those four local conditions is realisable by some mirror curve.

Download PDF File

Wallpaper groups and infinite or repeating kolams

When kolam-like motifs are repeated across the plane (or when infinite “endless” kolams are considered), the possible symmetries fall among the 17 wallpaper groups. Because of the square (or sometimes hexagonal) lattice underlying most pulli grids, the groups that appear most naturally are those compatible with 2-fold and 4-fold rotations and with orthogonal or diagonal mirrors: principally \(p2\), \(pmm\), \(p4\), \(p4m\), \(p4g\), and occasionally hexagonal groups when the underlying lattice allows it. The crystallographic restriction (only 2-, 3-, 4- or 6-fold rotations) is automatically satisfied by the grid.

Knot-Theoretic Approaches

Knot-theoretic and Temperley-Lieb approaches (Ishimoto, Jablan et al.) capture the topological monolinearity and crossing structure but do not by themselves classify the geometric symmetry group; the point-group or wallpaper analysis is independent of, and complementary to, the knot invariants.

We will follow the Lunda Geometry treatment of Gerdes here, and also briefly( Ha! Briefly!!) touch upon the S. Jablan’s treatment based on Knot Theory.

TBWU.

  • Discuss the similarity to Wang tiles.

Questions: - Can we generate random KSMs and find “symmetry on average”, in the manner of Field and Golubitsky? - Can we mimic Kolam Tiles / Saty Raghavachary’s video in code? - How “simple” can the code be?

Kolams with Code

Work in (slow….) Progress!!!

  • Using p5.js
  • Using R
Show the Code
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# ========== STEP 1: Canonical pieces ==========
# Each piece is a list of line segments inside the unit square [0,1]×[0,1]
# Ports: which sides it connects (N=1, E=2, S=3, W=4)

pieces <- list(
  straight_h = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0, 1), y = c(0.5, 0.5)), ports = c(2, 4)),
  straight_v = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0.5, 0.5), y = c(0, 1)), ports = c(1, 3)),
  turn_ne    = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0.5, 1), y = c(1, 0.5)), ports = c(1, 2)),
  turn_nw    = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0, 0.5), y = c(0.5, 1)), ports = c(1, 4)),
  turn_se    = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0.5, 1), y = c(0, 0.5)), ports = c(2, 3)),
  turn_sw    = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0, 0.5), y = c(0.5, 0)), ports = c(3, 4)),
  bounce_h   = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0, 0.5, 1), y = c(0.5, 0.3, 0.5)), ports = c(2, 4)), # mirror-like
  bounce_v   = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0.5, 0.3, 0.5), y = c(0, 0.5, 1)), ports = c(1, 3))
)

piece_names <- names(pieces)

# ========== STEP 2: Sampling & aligning ==========
m <- 6
n <- 8
set.seed(123)

# sample a piece for every cell
grid <- expand.grid(i = 1:n, j = 1:m) %>%
  mutate(piece = sample(piece_names, n(), replace = TRUE))

# expand into drawable segments, translated to cell position
draw_data <- grid %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  do({
    p <- pieces[[.$piece]]
    data.frame(
      i = .$i, j = .$j,
      x = p$segs$x + .$i - 1,
      y = p$segs$y + .$j - 1,
      group = paste(.$i, .$j, sep = "_")
    )
  }) %>%
  ungroup()

# optional: dots at cell centres (classic sona reference points)
dots <- expand.grid(x = 0.5:(n - 0.5), y = 0.5:(m - 0.5))

# plot
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = dots, aes(x, y), colour = "grey50", size = 2) +
  geom_path(
    data = draw_data, aes(x, y, group = group),
    colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Randomly sampled canonical pieces → sona/Kolam attempt")

Practical implications for design

Highest visual regularity is achieved by the group \(4mm_d\). Imposing a non-trivial point group dramatically reduces the number of free choices when assembling tiles or placing mirrors (exactly the content of Gopalan’s enumeration formulae). Lunda shading adds a second, independent layer of two-colour symmetry that can be present even when the underlying curve has lower geometric symmetry. For generative work the same constraints translate directly into rules on the Mirror Indicator Matrix or on the adjacency matrix of the step graph: the matrix (or its colouring) must be invariant under the desired group action.

These results give a complete, computationally usable catalogue of the symmetries that square-grid kolams and their Lunda colourings can possess.

Wait, But Why?

Kolams and Sona are powerful metaphors for graphs and networks. These ideas show up in a variety of situations, such as tranportation networks, supply-chain, friendship networks, tracing literary and artistic influence, and so on.
